dor-ansia-01.context: Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Mount to ordinary people who depended on the harvest and the day's wage. Before speaking of anxiety, he speaks of treasures and masters: what a person keeps as treasure ends up ruling the heart.
dor-ansia-01.focusQuestion: What have you been keeping as treasure, and what worry does it bring to your tomorrow?
dor-ansia-01.keywordGloss: What a person keeps as most valuable; for Jesus, it pulls the heart and can become a master.
facts: Where the treasure is, there the heart is.
No one can serve God and riches.
Birds neither sow nor reap, and the Father feeds them.
Worry does not add a cubit to life.
The Father knows what the disciples need.
Each day already brings its own trouble.

dor-ansia-02.context: Paul writes as a prisoner (Philippians 1:13) and thanks the church in Philippi for the help it sent. Before speaking of his own contentment, he shows the church what to do with anxiety: bring everything to God.
dor-ansia-02.focusQuestion: What do you feel you need to have in order to be at peace, and what would Paul say about it?
dor-ansia-02.keywordGloss: Being at peace with what you have, because strength comes from Christ, not from the circumstances.
facts: Paul says not to be anxious about anything.
Requests go to God with thanksgiving.
God's peace guards the heart and the mind.
Paul learned to be content in any situation.
Paul has known both plenty and hunger.

dor-ansia-03.context: David was a shepherd before he was king (1 Samuel 16:11). In Psalm 23 he uses what he knew of the work to speak of God: a shepherd who leads, feeds and protects, even when the path grows dark.
dor-ansia-03.focusQuestion: What valley are you in right now, and what changes when you know the shepherd walks with you in it?
dor-ansia-03.keywordGloss: One who leads, feeds and protects the sheep up close; the psalm gives this name to the Lord.
facts: The Lord is the psalmist's shepherd.
The shepherd makes the psalmist lie down in green pastures.
The shepherd leads in paths of righteousness.
The psalmist admits walking through the valley of the shadow of death.
The shepherd's rod and staff bring comfort.
Goodness and mercy follow the psalmist.

dor-ansia-04.context: Jesus teaches about prayer in the Sermon on the Mount, to people who knew long prayers meant to impress. A little later, in the same sermon, he speaks of anxiety about tomorrow (Matthew 6:34).
dor-ansia-04.focusQuestion: What would you ask God for if you prayed only for today?
dor-ansia-04.keywordGloss: The provision asked for the day; Jesus teaches us to depend on the Father today, without stockpiling tomorrow's fear.
facts: Jesus says not to use vain repetitions in prayer.
The Father knows what we need before we ask.
The prayer begins by calling God Father in heaven.
We ask that God's will be done on earth.
The bread is asked for today.

dor-ansia-05.context: Peter writes to Christians scattered across Asia Minor (1 Peter 1:1) who faced hostility because of their faith. Before speaking of suffering, he reminds them of what nothing can take from them.
dor-ansia-05.focusQuestion: What worry loses its grip when you remember that God keeps your inheritance and keeps you?
dor-ansia-05.keywordGloss: What God has reserved in heaven for his own, kept by him, just as he keeps the heirs themselves.
facts: God gave us new birth according to his great mercy.
The inheritance is reserved in heaven.
Those who believe are being guarded by God's power.
The readers rejoice, though grieved by trials.
Tested faith is more precious than gold.
